title: Mitigating Memorization Where It Happens
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: The token-level likelihood signal is heavy-tailed and sparse, so a small minority of isolated positions carries most of the signal.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; histogram left, bar plus cumulative curve right; callout boxes
description: Two side-by-side plots, both titled Qwen3-GSM8K. Panel (a) is a density histogram of the token-level signal ω_t = log p(x_t) − log p_ref(x_t). Teal bars lie at or below the mean and salmon bars above it. A teal density curve peaks sharply near zero and has a long right tail. A dashed vertical line marks the mean at 0.90. A teal callout says only 18.7% of tokens contribute to memorization, with skewness 2.89. Panel (b) is a bar chart of burst length, meaning the length of consecutive positive-signal runs. The bars are blue and shrink quickly from 60.8% at length 1 to 23.6%, 10.2% and 3.4%. A green cumulative-percentage curve rises toward 100% on a second axis. A cyan callout reads 84.4% ≤ 2 tokens, 0.8% > 5 tokens, mean 1.64. A small inset shows text snippets with red-highlighted tokens. The eye goes first to the tall left spike and the 60.8% bar.
caption: Token-level excess likelihood on Qwen3-GSM8K. (a) The distribution of $\omega_t$ is right-skewed (skewness $2.89$), with some positions exhibiting much larger target--reference likelihood differences than others. (b) Consecutive runs of positions with $\omega_t>0$ have a mean length of $1.64$; $60.8%$ of runs contain one position. These statistics describe the likelihood signal, rather than the lengths of memorized spans or ground-truth transitions between recall and generalization. Cross-setting concentration measurements are reported in Appendix [ref].
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce training sequences verbatim, raising privacy and copyright concerns. Existing mitigation methods apply interventions uniformly, often degrading predictions at the many positions unrelated to verbatim recall. We study a token-level log-likelihood ratio between a target model and a domain-competent reference with lower exposure to the evaluated sequences. Exposure-controlled experiments support its use for localizing positions associated with sequence-level verbatim recall. Across evaluated settings, a minority of positions carries a disproportionate share of the positive signal, motivating selective activation correction. From a first-order surrogate of the memorization-reduction objective, we derive a probe-steer framework, which decomposes intervention into a probe that flags high-signal activations and a steer that applies a correction only when the probe exceeds a threshold. We propose Gated Subspace Steering (GSS) as its practical instantiation: under a background normalization constraint, the probe-steer pairs that are optimal for this surrogate follow in closed form from the leading singular vectors of a whitened gradient-weighted activation matrix. Across four benchmarks, GSS achieves memorization suppression comparable to strong baselines, with favorable utility trade-offs in several settings, while requiring 10-100$\times$ less compute than optimization-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/ubc-tea/Mitigating-Memorization-Where-It-Happens.
